newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland loyalist extremists on warpath.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland loyalist extremists on warpath.

text.p: A maverick Northern Ireland Protestant extremist group, suspected of a string of attacks against Roman Catholic targets, on Thursday ruled out the possibility of declaring a ceasefire.
"The Loyalist Volunteer Force (LVF)... said it would not be in the interests of the Protestant people in Northern Ireland to call a ceasefire in any shape or form", the group said in a statement.

The LVF, fighting attempts to end British rule in Northern Ireland and reunite the province with the Irish Republic, poured scorn on a truce called on July 20 by its foes of the Irish Republican Army (IRA).

"The Protestant people must realise now this is another phoney ceasefire and final rush by the republican movement and the Irish government to bring the union down the road to a united Ireland," the statement said.

The statement, delivered to a Belfast news organisation with a recognised codeword, underlined tension caused by the killing of a 16-year-old boy last week in what police fear may have been a sectarian attack.

The Irish News, a newspaper read largely by Catholics, said on Monday police were hunting LVF activists in connection with the murder of James Morgan, whose body was found in a field near the village of Clough, south of Belfast.
He was abducted, beaten to death and dumped. No group has claimed responsibility for his death, the first since the IRA called a fresh halt to its war against British rule.

The LVF, which broke away from mainstream loyalist (pro-British) organisations after they declared a ceasefire in October 1994, is suspected of several attacks against offices of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein.

It also claimed responsibility for an attempted bomb attack in the Irish border town of Dundalk in June and threatened to kill Irish Catholics as part of a campaign to end the Dublin government's role as partner with Britain in efforts to find a negotiated solution to Northern Ireland's long-running conflict.
"The LVF has stated in the past that the Irish government will pay a heavy price for interfering in the internal affairs of Northern Ireland," the LVF statement said.

The statement urged Protestant loyalist and unionist organisations not to take any further part in Anglo-Irish peace talks, which will resume in earnest in September seeking to end a 28-year conflict that has killed 3,200 people.
Two unionist parties have walked out of the talks in protest at Britain's refusal to insist that the IRA hand over weapons as a condition for Sinn Fein's entry to the talks.

But two political parties close to loyalists still observing a ceasefire and the province's most powerful Protestant group, the Ulster Unionist Party led by David Trimble, have so far stayed at the negotiations.

Trimble has rejected Anglo-Irish proposals that disarmament discussions go in parallel with the negotiations and wants assurances that the IRA will be forced to hand over weaponry during the talks rather than just express readiness to do so.

Britain and Ireland are standing by their proposals, which has raised the prospect that Trimble may not sit down to negotiate with Sinn Fein at the first substantive talks on a settlement which start on September 15.
The IRA says it will not surrender a single bullet and accuses Britain of trying to turn talks on a political settlement into an attempt to disarm and disband it.
